etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French muse, from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet 85”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:
quote.text: My toung-tide Muſe in manners holds her ſtill,While comments of your praiſe richly compil'd,Reſerue their Character with goulden quill,And precious phraſe by all the Muſes fil’d.

quote.citation: 1637, John Milton, “Lycidas”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], published 1646, →OCLC:
quote.text: So may some gentle Muse With lucky words favour my destined urn

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English musen, from Old French muser.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become lost in thought, to ponder.
(transitive) To say (something) with due consideration or thought.
(transitive) To think on; to meditate on.

quote.text: Come, then, expressive Silence, muse his praise.

quote.citation: 2013 June 7, David Simpson, “Fantasy of navigation”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 26, page 36:
quote.text: It is tempting to speculate about the incentives or compulsions that might explain why anyone would take to the skies in [the] basket [of a balloon]: […];  […]; or perhaps to muse on the irrelevance of the borders that separate nation states and keep people from understanding their shared environment.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Muse not that I thus suddenly proceed; for what I will, I will, and there an end.

definitions.definition: An act of musing; a period of thoughtfulness.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: still he sate long time astonished / As in great muse, ne word to creature spake.

quote.citation: 1886 May 1 – July 31, Robert Louis Stevenson, Kidnapped, being Memoirs of the Adventures of David Balfour in the Year 1751: […], London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 1886, →OCLC:
quote.text: And with this Alan fell into a muse, and for a long time sate[sic] very sad and silent.

quote.citation: 1978, Lawrence Durrell, Livia, Faber & Faber 1992 (Avignon Quintet), p. 416:
quote.text: He fell into a muse and pulled his upper lip.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French musse. See muset.

definitions.definition: A gap or hole in a hedge, fence, etc. through which a wild animal is accustomed to pass; a muset.
